Replay

Explaining a local replay failure

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Canonical field differencesPersistent gameplay windows

audit reports the first tick whose re-executed state or event batch differs from recorded history. audit_capture performs the same single audit execution and retains the evidence at that first mismatch:

Odin
capture: r.Audit_Capture(World, Input, Event)
defer r.audit_capture_destroy(&capture)
result := r.audit_capture(&timeline, first_tick, &capture)
if capture.ready {
    // capture.parent: the preceding frame used to execute the failing tick
    // capture.input: the recorded input for that tick
    // capture.expected / capture.actual: independent owned frame values
    // capture.expected_events / actual_events: independent owned arrays
}

The capture is populated only for Diverged_State or Diverged_Event. Successful audit, missing history, invalid arguments and a step that aborts do not produce a capture. The returned Result still explains those errors. An occupied capture must be destroyed before reuse. Destroy even when no mismatch was captured; the operation is safe for an empty owner.

Captures do not alias the timeline, its recorded events or replay scratch. They remain available after another audit/correction reuses scratch, and modifying a capture cannot change the original history. All frame/input/event values still obey the core's no-reference value contract. Only the diagnostic event arrays allocate, and only after a divergence has actually been found. Ordinary audit retains its existing behavior and does not allocate a capture.

This is evidence from one local replay, not a proof of determinism or a recorder of illegal external side effects. Callbacks must still obey the simulation contract. The captured preceding frame and input help reproduce one tick with the same code and explicitly supplied model configuration; hidden external state is not captured.

Canonical field differences#

The optional replay/schema layer locates differing fields in schema-supported values. It remains separate from the core, whose value rules also permit types without a portable network schema.

Odin
schema: sc.Schema
sc.init(&schema, World)
defer sc.destroy(&schema)
fields: [32]sc.Difference
report := sc.diff(&schema, capture.expected.state, capture.actual.state, fields[:])
for field in fields[:report.count] {
    expected := sc.diff_value(&schema, field, .Left)
    actual := sc.diff_value(&schema, field, .Right)
    fmt.println(field.path, expected, actual)
    delete(expected); delete(actual)
}

report.total counts every differing field, while report.count is the number written into the caller's bounded buffer. Paths and enum names borrow the schema's metadata; keep it alive while using them. Formatted values are owned strings. Both complete inputs are validated before any output entry is written. Reports identify which side failed validation. Public projection excludes private fields from comparison and output. Compare authority fields only in trusted local tooling.

These are canonical scalar-bit differences: padding is ignored, endian-qualified fields are normalized, and signed zero or permitted NaN payload differences remain visible. The core audit compares logical Odin values, so its equality rule can differ from canonical byte equality. diff_encoded compares exact canonical payloads; validate framing/context/authenticity separately before supplying untrusted bytes.

For event failures, compare the captured event counts and use a schema for r.Occurrence(Event) to compare corresponding entries. Event order and semantic IDs are part of the core's recorded batch, so a different order is itself useful evidence.

The Scrapyard inspection tool shows the field-diff API applied to validated real game checkpoints. It emits bounded JSON without modifying either save or opening a network session.

audit_window finds the latest bounded replayable suffix without copying gameplay values. It stops at an initial/corrected checkpoint or retained-history edge. audit_recent captures a failure from that suffix. This is useful for clients, whose authority correction did not come from locally recorded generating input. The Godot overlay uses these boundaries and the owned plain-text formatter in replay/diagnostic for explicit developer audits.

Persistent gameplay windows#

Portable local recordings retain a complete replayable suffix, including input, expected frames and events. They can be exported from Hello, loaded by the headless verifier and executed in native/WASM independently of the original process. This complements the failure-only Audit_Capture and transport-interface trace recorder.

Loaded recording playback adds a transactional recording owner and expected-frame cursor. Hello's Open recording control verifies files, shows mismatch details, and explicitly returns to the original game or starts a new branch. Native and Chrome import workflows preserve pause and effect ownership.
